chunks.content: Essential Points Radiation is a risk factor for thyroid cancer; the risk steadily increases up to the dose of 10 Gy, levels off in the 10- to 30-Gy interval, and asymptotically declines at higher doses but remains elevated; once exposed, the risk persists for many decades Risks from the external and internal irradiation are comparable There is no evidence of dose–response departure from linearity at low doses (<0.1 Gy) and of the existence of a “safe” threshold dose The magnitude of radiation risk for thyroid cancer is highest if exposure takes place at a young age After the Chornobyl nuclear reactor accident, due to internal exposure to radioactive iodine, a dramatic increase in the incidence of childhood thyroid cancers was observed, especially among children less than 5 years old at the time of the accident Although many thyroid cancers were found by the thyroid-screening program after the Fukushima nuclear power plant accident, comparisons of exposures and characteristics of thyroid cancer diagnosed after the Chornobyl and Fukushima nuclear accidents do not support a causative role of radiation in the latter Reduction of the risk for thyroid cancer may be achieved by following the As Low As Reasonably Achievable principle, and iodine thyroid blockage may be performed to protect from anticipated internal exposure Radiation Exposure and Risk for Thyroid Cancer Thyroid Cancer After Radiation Exposure The idea about a possible association between radiation exposure at infancy and thyroid cancer dates back to the 1950s. A seminal paper by Duffy and Fitzgerald reported that among 28 patients with thyroid cancer 18 years or younger at diagnosis, 10 had a history of radiological treatment with X-rays for enlargement of the thymus at 4 to 16 weeks of age ( ). Within the next decade and a half, a series of studies with a retrospective design provided further circumstantial evidence of a link between irradiation and subsequent development of thyroid cancer later in life in the form of complementary statements ( ) that “(a) groups of thyroid cancer patients have a substantially higher incidence of irradiation in their histories and (b) groups of patients who have received radiation therapy have a substantially higher incidence of thyroid cancer” ( ). One of these studies estimated the period of latency (ie, the time between irradiation and diagnosis of thyroid cancer) in a group of 528 thyroid cancer patients who had previously received external beam therapy when they were <1 to >30 years of age, had a mean of 12.5 years, and a median of 10 years, ranging from 1 to >30 years ( ). The first work on thyroid cancer in the Hiroshima A-bomb hibakusha used data collected in 1958-1959 from the members of the Adult Health Study ( ), more than a decade after the bombing in August, 1945. The study did not find a statistically significant risk association between those exposed to higher and lower radiation doses, or between the individuals who had been irradiated at different distances from the hypocenter, although the prevalence of thyroid cancer was higher in those proximally exposed. “Superficial examination of the gross data,” however, was suggestive of the possibility of a relationship between irradiation and thyroid cancer. It is worth noting that this study was based on 12 cases only and did not include cases from Nagasaki. Furthermore, since Tumor Registries were established in Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1957 and 1958, respectively ( ), it is quite possible that some cancers that had occurred earlier were not included. Radiation risk for thyroid cancer in A-bomb hibakusha has been confirmed in later studies as discussed below. These historical examples of a link between radiation and thyroid cancer illustrate the external irradiation circumstances such as exposure of patients for medical indications or accidental irradiation of the population. After radioactive iodine (RAI) isotopes became widely available in 1946 ( ), exposure of the thyroid to internal radiation became a possibility. The thyroid is physiologically avid for iodine, therefore RAI isotope uptake, whether intentional or nonintentional, is intrinsically associated with radiation risk. Here, we attempt to review the effects of external and internal exposures on thyroid cancer risk, including factors that may modify it, and address the risk from different radiation doses. “radiation dose” is a broad term that needs to be considered from several points of view. First, the “dose” reflects the amount of energy deposited per unit mass of the matter (body, organ, and tissue) by different kinds of “hot particles.” The absorbed dose is literally the amount of energy (measured in Joules, J) deposited per kilogram of the matter, thus J/kg = Gy (Gray), and when applied to biological objects such as humans may indicate the extent of molecular and biochemical changes caused by irradiation. Second, “hot particles” may be of different quality such as photons (eg, X-rays, γ-rays), electrons (β-particles), protons, α-particles (helium nuclei), neutrons, heavy ions, etc., and of different energy, which have different damaging potentials. To account for this, different types of radiation are assigned dimensionless radiation weighting factors, which is 1 for photons and electrons, 5 for protons, and 20 for α-particles and heavy ions; for neutrons of different energy the factor is bell-shaped with a minimum of 5 and maximum of 20 ( ). A simple product of the absorbed dose (in Gy) and radiation weighting factor would yield the equivalent dose measured in Sieverts (Sv). For instance, if a patient with nasopharyngeal carcinoma undergoes an external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) with a prescribed dose of 50 Gy of X-rays (and the thyroid is fully in the projection of the beam), then the equivalent dose to the thyroid would be 50 Gy × 1 (1 is the radiation weighting factor for X-rays) = 50 Sv. Both the absorbed dose and the equivalent dose are applicable to individual tissues and organs. Third, to estimate the overall potential detriment from radiation exposure, it is necessary to take into account radiation sensitivity of different organs. For this purpose, the organs are ascribed the so-called tissue weighting factors so that their sum is 1 (ie, the whole body) ( ). In the hypothetical EBRT example above, the following tissues would likely be exposed: the skin (∼10%), the brain (∼30%), bone marrow (∼5%), salivary glands (∼100%), and the thyroid (∼100%), which have tissue weighting factors of 0.01, 0.01, 0.12, 0.01, and 0.04, respectively. Recalling that radiation weighting factor for X-rays is 1, one can first calculate the equivalent doses for each organ, accounting for the proportion of the tissue exposed: 50 Gy × 1 × 0.1 (10%) = 5 Sv for the skin, 50 Gy × 1 × 0.3 (30%) = 15 Sv for the brain, 50 Gy × 1 × 0.05 (5%) = 2.5 Sv for the bone marrow, 50 Gy × 1 × 1 (100%) = 50 Sv for salivary glands, and 50 Gy × 1 × 1 (100%) = 50 Sv for the thyroid. Then, the equivalent doses for each organ are multiplied by corresponding tissue weighting factors: 5 Sv × 0.01 = 0.05 Sv for the skin, 15 Sv × 0.01 = 0.15 Sv for the brain, 2.5 Sv × 0.12 = 0.3 Sv for the bone marrow, 50 Sv × 0.01 = 0.5 Sv for salivary glands, and 50 Sv × 0.04 = 2 Sv for the thyroid. These values are summed up: 0.05 (skin) + 0.15 (brain) + 0.3 (bone marrow) + 0.5 (salivary glands) + 2 (thyroid) = 3 Sv. The result, 3 Sv, comprises the so-called effective dose (also measured in Sv), which is useful to compare potential risks (effects) from different radiological treatment modalities (eg, EBRT or medical imaging of different anatomical areas) or different exposure scenarios, but is not applicable to an organ, and is not intended to estimate individual risk from the exposure ( ). However, if one reads, for instance, that the annual effective dose received by a person from a homogeneous whole-body exposure to γ-rays was 2 mSv, it could be tentatively inferred that the absorbed and equivalent doses to the thyroid were also around 2 mGy and 2 mSv, respectively, from this exposure. Such estimates are, nevertheless, imprecise and are not advisable in scientific research. With technological advances and growing understanding of sources of radiation over time, the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) classified radiation exposures into medical, occupational, and public categories and planned, existing, and emergency situations ( ). The following subsection considers exposures taking place according to different scenarios and stemming from various combinations of exposure categories and exposure situations. Radiation Doses and Thyroid Doses From Different Radiation Exposure Categories and Situations Planned medical exposures According to the World Health Organization, more than 3600 million diagnostic radiology, and 37 million nuclear medicine procedures are performed annually ( ). Diagnostic radiology procedures In a recent study of medical radiation exposures in the United States, among diagnostic radiology procedures the highest patient doses were from computed tomography (CT), 63% of the collective effective dose, while those from radiography and fluoroscopy amounted to 10% ( ).

Diagnostic radiology procedures In a recent study of medical radiation exposures in the United States, among diagnostic radiology procedures the highest patient doses were from computed tomography (CT), 63% of the collective effective dose, while those from radiography and fluoroscopy amounted to 10% ( ). Principally, externally delivered X-rays are the source of radiation in these procedures. presents data on the thyroid absorbed doses in adults ( , ), and children ( , ) from different diagnostic radiological exposures in 2000-2010. Most radiographic and dental radiological examinations, and CT scans deliver thyroid doses ranging from a fraction of mGy to a few mGy. However, the doses are higher from those procedures in which the thyroid is localized in or is close to the field to be imaged. These are the neck, thoracic, ribs, and cervical spine radiography, esophageal fluoroscopy, and heart, cervical spine, and chest CT, from which the thyroid may be exposed to some 5 to 35 mGy. It should be noted that thyroid doses from diagnostic radiological procedures markedly decreased from the 1960s to the 1990s (eg, about 10-fold for the scull and cervical radiography) and remained relatively unchanged from the 2000s. Exceptions from this general trend are the cervical spine and chest involving CT, which demonstrated a moderate dose increase (from ∼20 mGy to ∼30 mGy) from 1995 to 2005 ( ). Note also that in children, the doses from head CT are higher than in adults, and decline with age (from 20 mGy in a newborn to 3 mGy mean dose in an adult, as of 2001), while those from the chest CT are somewhat lower and do not markedly change (18 mGy in a newborn and to 22 mGy mean dose in an adult, as of 2001) ( ). In children, the thyroid doses from head CT scans did not change much or became just slightly lower during the 3 decades from 1990 to 2010; in contrast, doses from chest examinations declined several fold ( ). To date, a number of web-based effective dose calculators from CT scans are available, although the number of software tools for an organ (including the thyroid) dose calculation for patients of different age is rather limited, and most are commercial, as reviewed in ( ). A free tool, the National Cancer Institute dosimetry system for CT, is also available ( , ). Diagnostic nuclear medicine procedures Radioisotopes are widely used to examine the functional state of, or to image, an organ/tissue. Typically, radioactive tracers used for diagnostic or pretreatment procedures are short-lived low linear energy transfer isotopes emitting γ-rays or positrons enabling detection with gamma camera/planar scintigraphy or single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), or positron emission tomography (PET) machines. Radiopharmaceuticals taken orally or, more commonly, injected intravenously (thus, internal exposure) are preferentially or specifically accumulated in the target organ as determined by a vehicle molecule/probe/ligand to which a radioisotope is coupled. When the thyroid is not a target tissue, it may be exposed to scatter radiation from a nearby target organ or from the circulation. In addition, uptake of an isotope may take place due to metabolic or radiochemical breakdown of a radiopharmaceutical; if such a possibility exists, thyroid blocking agents may be used especially for iodine- or technetium-containing radiopharmaceuticals. In general, radiation doses to the thyroid from procedures not targeting the thyroid are relatively low ( ), although brain scans, cancer detection (usually PET/CT), and cardiological procedures may deliver some 7 to 10 mGy ( , ). To achieve a better quality of imaging, hybrid procedures that combine SPECT or PET with CT (SPECT/CT or PET/CT, respectively) are frequently used. Radiation doses from the these procedures include both radioisotope and CT exposures. Radiation doses from nuclear medicine procedures targeting the thyroid are noticeably higher than from other examinations. Evaluation of thyroid functional state/physiology examines the sodium iodine symporter–mediated thyroid uptake/metabolism of a radioisotope with or without imaging. Gamma-emitting isotopes are used for this purpose. At present, 123 I is the preferable application because of the possibility of concurrent thyroid imaging and lower radiation exposure of a patient. The effective dose from 200 μCi of 123 I (a typical minimum activity administered to an adult patient) would be expected to be as low as 1.5 mSv ( ). 131 I and 99m Tc-pertechnetate may also be used depending on medical center policies/practices and isotope availability, delivering doses similar or just slightly higher than those from 123 I. During the last several decades, the weighted average absorbed dose from a thyroid uptake procedure (when usage of all 3 isotopes were considered) was estimated to be about 60 mGy ( ). This would result in an effective dose of about 2.4 mSv (given the thyroid tissue weighting factor of 0.04) which is comparable with the above-mentioned effective dose from 123 I-only procedures. Note also that 99m Tc-pertechnetate may not fully reflect thyroid function because it is captured by the gland but is not organified in contrast to sodium iodide. Thyroid scan or thyroid scintigraphy involves imaging and is used to evaluate thyroid structure and function in various thyroid diseases, to visualize hot or cold thyroid nodules of malignant or benign nature, ectopic thyroid tissue, metastasis or recurrence, and to facilitate a decision on RAI therapy and its radioisotope dosage. 123 I, 99m Tc-pertechnetate, and 131 I are most commonly used, and imaging is performed with a planar gamma-camera or SPECT/CT. Recently, a meta-analysis found 124 I PET/CT to be effective for identifying differentiated thyroid cancer lesions, in some instances overperforming the post-RAI therapy 131 I scan ( ). The activity of radioisotopes for a thyroid scan is usually several fold higher than for uptake examination, which may result in thyroid doses exceeding 100 mGy, which are the highest among all diagnostic nuclear medicine procedures ( ). To illustrate how thyroid scans add to the absorbed thyroid dose, data from the United States Radiologic Technologist (USRT) study may be used. For instance, cumulative doses from different diagnostic examinations excluding thyroid scans in subjects not diagnosed for thyroid cancer were from 0 to 1853 mGy (average, 26 mGy), and from 0 to 34 313 mGy (average, 65 mGy) when thyroid examinations were considered ( ). Therapeutic exposures to external beam radiation EBRT may be performed for malignant or benign conditions. Depending on the tumor or lesion localization, some EBRT may result in irradiation of the thyroid. Although EBRT may be prescribed to patients of any age, most data in the literature are from relatively young patients. This is explained by the fact that even though EBRT may impose radiation-related risk for thyroid disease, the period of latency of such a disease may be quite long, exceeding survival time of a cancer patient who had received EBRT or his/her natural lifespan if treatment took place at an older age. If a cancer patient undergoes EBRT at childhood/young age and survives, the follow-up duration may be sufficient to obtain reliable information on thyroid status. Therefore, studies commonly reported patients diagnosed for primary cancers before age 20-21 years ( ). The most common types of cancer, treatment of which includes EBRT, are hematological malignancies (acute leukemias), Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, central nervous system malignancies (medulloblastoma), head and neck cancer (nasopharyngeal carcinoma), soft tissue/bone tumors (Ewing sarcoma), neuroblastoma, and Wilms tumor ( , ). Radiation doses to the thyroid from EBRT with prescribed doses of 23 to 80 Gy may reach some 5 to 70 Gy and cause hypothyroidism ( ). EBRT for breast cancer with prescribed doses of 20 to 50 Gy may deliver substantially lower doses of 35 to 140 mGy ( , ). Benign conditions for which EBRT was used during the 1920s to 1970s were enlarged thymus, tinea capitis, lymphoid hyperplasia/tonsils/adenoids, and hemangioma ( , ). Estimated exposure doses to the thyroid varied from 0 to 28 Gy and did not exceed 0.5 Gy for most instances, being noticeably lower than those from EBRT for cancer. The therapeutic effect is due to beta-radiation, which can penetrate soft tissues to 0.6 to 2 mm ( ). Internal therapeutic exposures The major thyroid exposures from internal radiation in clinical settings occur from RAI therapy with 131 I for hyperthyroidism developing in the course of Graves disease, toxic adenoma, or toxic multinodular goiter; in some cases, RAI may be given for nontoxic multinodular goiter. The therapeutic effect is due to beta-radiation, which can penetrate soft tissues to 0.6 to 2 mm ( ). The purpose of RAI therapy is to cause tissue reaction (partial destruction) eventually leading to thyroid volume reduction, allowing one to control hyperthyroidism. Recommended RAI activity for Graves disease is 370 to 555 MBq (10-15 mCi; 50-200 μCi/g thyroid tissue) in individual or fixed regimens ( , ). There is a strong correlation between the administered activity and absorbed dose to the thyroid ( ), which may range from 50 to over 400 Gy, and the desired outcome appears to be proportional to the dose ( ). Absorbed doses to the thyroid from RAI treatment of toxic adenoma or toxic multinodular goiter are even higher than those in Graves disease since recommended activity is 150 to 200 μCi/g thyroid tissue. It can be anticipated that thyroid irradiation may also occur during targeted treatments (eg, for cancer) that employ radiopharmaceuticals. In case an agent is RAI based, such as 131 I-MIBG for neuroendocrine tumors ( ), thyroid blocking is recommended. In a prospective study of 33 pediatric patients with neuroblastoma who received the first dose of 666 MBq/kg 131 I-MIBG therapy after potassium iodide and levothyroxine pretreatment, mean absorbed dose to the thyroid was 0.16 mGy/MBq of administered activity ( ) as calculated using the OLINDA (Organ Level Internal Dose Assessment) dosimetry software ( ). Conceivably, the absorbed thyroid dose might have reached several Gy in a child weighing 25 kg, but it needs to be borne in mind that the disease subjected to high-dose 131 I-MIBG therapy is life-threatening, thus radiation-related risk for the thyroid might not be of primary concern at the time of treatment. Follow-up care for survivors should certainly include thyroid function and nodularity examinations. Occupational planned exposures Exposures to ionizing radiation may take place in the course of work associated with the usage of sources of radiation such as nuclear and general industry, medical, research and/or education institutions, military facilities, and others. For most instances, irradiation is from external high-energy low linear energy transfer γ-rays (or X-rays), less commonly from neutrons and β-particles, and is incurred during work, hence exposed subjects are adult employees of various age. The effective dose limit for occupational exposures recommended by the ICRP is 20 mSv, averaged over defined periods of 5 years with no single year exceeding 50 mSv ( ). In this regard it is necessary to remember that the thyroid has a tissue weighting factor of 0.04 ( ), thus contributing 1/25 of the total potential health detriment from a certain equivalent dose uniformly delivered to the body. Different investigations of occupational exposures, especially of nuclear workers, usually report the cumulative absorbed, effective, or equivalent doses, and only some present the organ/tissue doses. According to the analysis of 14 occupational exposure studies (1 of which was the USRT cohort, while most of the others included nuclear workers from different countries, and also Chornobyl cleanup workers and US atomic veterans), cumulative doses ranged from 0 to 2.6 Gy with mean doses from 6 to 82 mSv (or mGy) (the highest values were in the Chornobyl cleanup workers), and those exceeding 100 mSv (or mGy) were recorded in <1% to 22% of the participants ( ). The mean individual annual equivalent dose of 1.7 mSv (median 0.4 mSv; 0.9-2.3 mSv, range) was found in a study of nuclear workers in France, the United Kingdom, and the United States ( ). A mean cumulative dose of about 20 mSv with that exceeding 50 mSv in 10% was recorded in industrial radiographers ( ). Planned occupational exposures also occur in physicians, radiographers, nurses, and medical physicists involved in radiology, radiation oncology, nuclear medicine, and interventional radiology. Annual effective doses depend on the specialty and role, type of procedure(s), corresponding administered activity and exposure time, workload, skills, and usage of protective garments/shields and drapes, and may vary from a fraction of mSv to several mSv ( ). Median equivalent occupational dose to the thyroid from 9 types of different interventional medical procedures in 14 hospitals in Germany was determined to be 4.1 μSv (730 μSv, maximum) per procedure ( ). Mean cumulative absorbed thyroid dose of 64 mGy (median 40 mGy, 0.16-2300 mGy, range) was reported in USRT cohort members who worked between 1916 and 1997 ( ), and 10 mGy (median 1.4 mGy, 0.007-9861 mGy, range) in South Korean medical radiation workers for the period from 1996 to 2015 ( ). Astronauts and cockpit aircrew are also exposed to radiation, although of natural origin. Astronauts experience galactic cosmic radiation (mostly protons, helium, and heavy metal nuclei, and some beta-particles and positrons) ( ), solar particle events (mostly protons), and the Earth's radiation belts (mostly protons and electrons) since the astronaut is not protected by the Earth’s atmosphere and magnetic field. The typical effective dose rate inside the International Space Station is 0.5 to 1 mSv/day (0.2-0.5 mGy) ( ). With regard to thyroid doses, a study employing passive dosimeter packages provided by the National Space Development Agency of Japan and placed inside a human phantom torso, which was flown in the cargo bay of the Shuttle mission in June 1998 for 9.8 days, found a dose rate of 214 μGy/day, resulting in an absorbed dose of 2.2 mGy, and equivalent dose of 4 mSv ( ). Aircraft crew were estimated to acquire average annual effective doses of 1.2 to 5 mSv, maximum 6 to 7 mSv ( ), depending on the flight time, routes, altitude, and solar activity (eg, high-energy protons produce neutrons after collisions in the upper atmosphere). The distribution of annual effective doses has a bell-shaped form, with the maximum between 1.5 and 2.5 mSv ( ). Although there are no thyroid dose estimates, it should be taken into account that the whole body is evenly exposed in these conditions. Public exposures Planned exposures Planned public exposures assume irradiation of the general public from sources other than the natural background. The ICRP recommends a dose limit of 1 mSv in such situations ( ). Typical examples of planned exposures to the public would be living near nuclear facilities such as nuclear plants or fuel-cycle plants, which may release or emit small amounts of radioactivity to the environment during normal operations. These releases usually occur in the form of gaseous or liquid effluents and may lead to internal or external exposures. The major isotopes contributing to the collective dose from nuclear plant releases are 3 H and 134,137 Cs ( ), although many other species, including noble gases and 131 I, are released ( ). Studies in Germany and in the United States found very low annual effective doses to the residents at the μSv scale ( , ) with the highest dose to the thyroid of infants of 9 μSv ( ). External exposures of family members or caregivers may take place at the residence or places where patients stay after receiving radiotherapy with unsealed agents such as RAI, (eg, for thyrotoxicosis or thyroid cancer) during the outpatient phase. In such cases, exposures are not subject to dose limits since they are considered to be medical and are recommended not to exceed 5 mSv during the treatment period (1 mSv for children ( )); in the EU, proposed dose constraints are 1 mSv for children, 3 mSv for adults up to 60 years old, and 15 mSv for older family members ( ). A number of studies reported the effective external doses to family members from 0 to some 8 mSv, although the mean doses usually did not exceed 1 mSv, and the vast majority were less than 5 mSv, as reviewed recently ( ). Of note, the individual doses did not correlate with RAI activity administered to the patient, and the highest/lowest doses were mostly determined by the behavior patterns of family members. The potential doses from internal exposures for family members of patients receiving RAI therapy are considered to be very low compared with external ones. The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission conservatively set the fractional intake (the fraction of the activity administered to the patient that would be taken in by the individual exposed to the patient) of unsealed radioactive material to 10 −5 ( ). Patient release criteria are regulated by national bodies, and vary from country to country (eg, from 2.0 mCi in Germany to 13 mCi in Japan and 33.0 mCi in the United States). Given the factor of 10 −5 , a family member of a patient administered 30 mCi of 131 I may intake about 0.3 μCi and receive an effective dose of 0.3 mSv ( ). Therefore, particular attention should be paid to avoid prolonged stay in proximity to the patient, especially for children ( ). Existing exposures Existing exposure situations assume exposures from already present sources such as radon or other environmental radioactive isotopes or cosmic rays, naturally occurring radioactive material (NORM), and radiocontaminated areas. Effects of these sources have been analyzed in detail elsewhere ( ). Here, we present some selected or relevant scenarios, although thyroid doses from those remain largely unaddressed. Radon, a noble gas and an α-particle emitter ( 222 Rn) is the greatest contributor (∼50%) to individual radiation doses from natural sources, totaling about 1.3 mSv (0.2-10 mSv) of the annual effective dose ( ). Other terrestrial sources include uranium and thorium series radionuclides, and potassium-40 ( 40 K isotope); estimated external individual effective dose from those account for about 0.5 mSv per year, and about 0.3 mSv from ingestion. Cosmic rays may add about 0.4 mSv annually. In total, average global effective dose to the public from natural sources is about 2.4 mSv, but no data are available on the specific contribution of different types to the radiation dose burden to the thyroid. Radiation doses to passengers on aircraft, especially frequent flyers, may also be regarded as an example of public exposure under existing situations. Similarly to aircrew members described above, passengers encounter irradiation of the whole body by cosmic rays. Average effective dose rates vary from 2 μSv/h for a transequatorial flight to 6.8 μSv/h for a transatlantic or transpolar flight ( ) but may change depending on solar activity. Exposure to NORM may occur for residents of areas with industries performing ore and coal mining, gas and oil drilling, and some other technologies, wastes or byproducts which become components of the environment. Exposures to NORM may be external and internal, and are considered to cause very small increases in annual effective doses to the public in the range of μSv for most instances ( ). Emergency exposures Emergency situations may arise after a nuclear explosion or radiological accident, either minor or major, when both occupational and public categories of exposure may take place. Emergency exposures to the public after the Chornobyl and Fukushima accidents are presented in separate sections. Here, the examples of public exposure in emergencies, are the August 1945 A-bombings of Japan, the 1957 fire at Windscale reactor in the United Kingdom, the Three Mile Island nuclear power station accident of 1979, the Marshall Islands Castle Bravo thermonuclear test in March 1954, atmospheric nuclear weapon tests at the Nevada (1951-1962), Semipalatinsk (1949-1961), Lop Nor (1964-1980), and French Polynesia (1970-1974) test sites, and releases from the Hanford test site in the mid-1940s to 1950s. Perhaps, the best-known emergency exposures to the public are the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August, 1945, with the 16-kiloton 235 U- and 21-kiloton 239 Pu-based devices, respectively. The immediate death toll and the number of people who died during 1945 accounted for about 140 000 and 74 000 people in the 2 cities ( , ), which is approximately one-third of the populations of the cities. The Atomic Bomb Casualty Commission was established in 1946, then reorganized to the Radiation Effect Research Foundation (RERF) in 1975 “to undertake a long range, continuing study of the biological and medical effects of the atomic bomb on man” ( ). Since 1950, a cohort of the Life Span Study (LSS) has been established, which includes about 94 000 survivors (<10 km from the hypocenters) from Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and 27 000 not-in-city individuals ( ). Careful dosimetry systems were developed, and currently in use is the DS02R1, which contains individual dose estimates for 15 organs ( ). Unshielded weighted radiation doses from the initial (γ-rays and neutrons) and residual radiation (fallouts and neutron-activated materials) were about 7 and 10 Gy at 1 km from the hypocenters, and 13 mGy and 23 mGy at 2.5 km in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, respectively ( ). The distribution of individual thyroid doses in the LSS cohort demonstrates that in about 43% of its members those were <5 mGy, 5 to 99 mGy in 34%, 100 to 249 mGy in 9%, 250 to 499 mGy in 5%, and 500 to 999 mGy and ≥1 Gy in about 4.5% each ( ). The LSS cohort is the largest source of data on radiation health effects from acute exposures to external radiation, which laid the ground for the modern system of radiological protection. The absorbed thyroid doses from the radioactive releases at Windscale in 1957 accounted for 0.01 Gy in local adults and 0.1 Gy in children and did not exceed 1 mGy at distant places ( ). The Three Mile Island accident of 1979 resulted in low doses with the estimated average effective doses from γ-rays of 0.09 mSv and maximum 0.25 mSv; since RAIs were also present among the released isotopes, thyroid doses in some individuals might have been relatively high ( ). The Castle Bravo test on the Marshall Islands, due to a sudden change in wind direction, led to irradiation of several hundred inhabitants of nearby atolls who might have received the average equivalent thyroid doses of 12 Sv for adults, and 52 Sv for 1-year-old children from external γ-radiation, and iodine and tellurium radioisotopes ( ). To quantify the magnitude of risk and/or impact of one or another factor, a number of measures of association between “exposure” and “outcome” have been proposed. The OR is the ratio of the odds (the number of events of interest in relation to the number of nonevents) occurring in the groups under comparison (eg, in an “exposed” and a control group). The OR is a metric useful for analysis of the effect of a factor of interest (eg, radiation exposure) once outcomes are known (eg, thyroid cancer occurred or not). For instance, if an OR for radiation exposure is calculated, it is possible to judge whether this factor was observed with a higher (or lower) frequency among individuals with thyroid cancer than among individuals without thyroid cancer (recall the first historical example in section “Thyroid Cancer After Radiation Exposure”). The OR is the statistic of choice in case–control studies. The RR (risk can be also regarded as “probability”) is the ratio of the number of events of interest (eg, thyroid cancer) in relation to the total number of events plus nonevents (ie, individuals with and without thyroid cancer) in an exposed (eg, to radiation) group and in a control (nonexposed) group. The RR is easy to understand because it clearly demonstrates whether exposure has an effect on outcomes. RRs are usually reported in cohort studies but cannot be used for case–control designs. Generally, the analyzed groups should be large enough, ideally being reasonably representative of the population, to produce a meaningful RR. ORs can also be reported in the cohort and cross-sectional studies, and if an event of interest is rare (conservatively, if its rate is less than 10%), ORs adequately approximate RRs ( ). Both RRs and ORs deal with the cumulative numbers of events and nonevents at the end of a study period. The IRR is the ratio of event rates in 2 groups or populations (eg, exposed and nonexposed). Incidence rate is calculated as the number of events (eg, thyroid cancer) registered during the study period divided by the total person-time at risk for disease (or by the average size of the group at risk for disease) during the study period in a given group. Some studies report the SIR, which is the ratio between the number of events in a given group (eg, population of an area contaminated by radioactive fallout) and the number of events expected in a larger reference population (eg, a whole nation). The SRR is the event rate in the groups or populations under study with the same distribution of characteristics that are intended to be controlled (eg, age, gender); to achieve standardization, a chosen reference population stratified for these characteristics is used. Standardization facilitates the comparison across the groups with different composition by putting them on the same scale. The IRR, SIR, and SRR can be obtained in cohort studies. Another measure that concerns the rate of events is the HR. Hazard is the probability that an event of interest occurs in an individual at a given time point of the study period. Accordingly, the HR indicates how often an event of interest (eg, thyroid cancer) takes place in 1 group (eg, exposed to radiation) compared with another (eg, nonexposed) over the study period. HRs are computed using different models belonging to the family of survival analysis methods. Although the HR apparently relates to the time scale, it should not be misinterpreted as an estimate how faster (or slower) the event will occur in one or another group. Instead, it is a magnitude of a chance that the event will occur at any time point of the study period in the carriers vs noncarriers of a given characteristic (eg, exposed vs nonexposed individuals). The HR is used in cohort, cross-sectional, and case–control studies addressing the rate of events. Dose–response assessment is used to determine the magnitude of risk (either relative or absolute) per dose unit. Such estimates can be obtained if the dose parameter (typically, on the Gy or mGy scale) is entered in a model. The model coefficient (sometimes referred to “beta” or “slope” in the linear models) for the dose term quantifies the impact of exposure on outcome. Diagnostic medical procedures Radiation risk for thyroid cancer from diagnostic X-ray exposures was statistically significant (OR 1.52, 95% CI 1.13-20.4) in a meta-analysis by Han et al ( ). Among different procedures, effects of CT scans (OR 1.46, 95% CI 1.27-1.68) and dental X-rays (OR 1.69, 95% CI 1.17-2.44) were elevated. The latter association was confirmed in a separate meta-analysis in which data sets partly overlapped with the Han study (pooled RR 1.87, 95% CI 1.11-3.15) ( ). A large-scale study in Taiwan reported an increased risk for thyroid cancer (OR 2.55, 95% CI 2.36-2.75) from CT scans with a positive dose–response ( ). Based on the BEIR VII models ( ), individual risk for thyroid cancer due to CT scans in adults was estimated to generally be <0.01% (10 per 100 000), although the estimates increased for younger individuals ( ). Interestingly enough, a national health insurance–wide Korean study ( ) found elevated risks for thyroid cancer from the higher number of CT scans (OR 1.09, 95% CI 1.03-1.16), and particularly from thyroid-exposing procedures (OR 1.28, 95% CI 1.05-1.57); the number of outpatient visits per year was also positively associated with the risk (OR 1.03, 95% CI 1.02-1.03). When the frequency of outpatient visits was accounted for in statistical models, the associations between thyroid cancer and the number of CT scans (OR 1.03, 95% CI 0.97-1.10) or those thyroid exposing (OR 1.14, 95% CI 0.93-1.41) were lost. The authors suggested that CT scans in adults are not an independent risk factor for thyroid cancer when the health care utilization rate is considered. Diagnostic chest X-rays (OR 1.66, 95% CI 0.99-2.78) and mammography (OR 1.04, 95% CI 0.92-1.17) did not confer elevated risk ( ). The lifetime attributable risk for thyroid cancer (the cumulative probability of developing cancer due to a given dose of radiation over the expected lifespan) from a breast dose of 4.7 mGy from a single screening examination of a 40-year-old woman was estimated to be 6 per 1 000 000 000 (or 1 in 166 million) ( ). In the prospective USRT cohort, exposures from individual diagnostic procedures that included dental X-rays, X-rays of the collar bone and shoulder, mammography, and thyroid scans were analyzed, and the risk for thyroid cancer was found to be nonsignificant when thyroid scans were not included (ERR/Gy: 2.29, 95% CI −0.91-7.01 after a 5-year latency), and statistically significant when thyroid scans were included (ERR/Gy 1.66, 95% CI 0.78-2.81) ( ). Therapeutic exposures Radiation doses to the thyroid from therapeutic exposures such as EBRT may range from low (<100 mGy) to very high (>70 Gy) depending on the disease under treatment, exposure regimens, and prescribed dose. The pooled analysis of 12 studies, 11 of which were EBRTs for malignant or benign conditions delivered in 1920-1986 to patients aged 0-19 years who received thyroid doses from >0 to 76 Gy (the highest doses were in childhood cancer patients), found significant RRs for thyroid cancer at 1 Gy across the studies, ranging from 2.0 (95% CI 1.3-4.3) to 22.0 (95% CI 14.1-34.7) ( ). Of importance, a curvilinear arc-shaped dependence of the RR estimates on the dose was observed: the risk increased in the dose range up to 10 Gy, plateaued out in the 10 to 30 Gy interval (RR 30-40), and then declined, yet remained significantly elevated at the doses >40 Gy ( ). Risk leveling-off at high doses is thought to be due to a cell killing effect. A similar shape of the dose–response was observed in the cohorts of childhood cancer survivors from the United States and France ( , ). RAI therapy is also used for some noncancer thyroid diseases, for instance hyperthyroidism. The activities are usually within the 370 to 555 MBq (10-15 mCi) range ( , ). A meta-analysis published 2 years ago claimed a nonsignificant pooled incidence ratio of 1.02 (95% CI 0.95-1.08) for all cancers in patients who received RAI based on the results of 12 studies ( ). The only type of malignancy for which the risk was statistically significantly increased was thyroid cancer (incidence ratio 1.86, 95% CI 1.19-2.92). Thyrotoxicosis due to Graves disease has been associated with thyroid cancer in several studies ( ), therefore the possibility of an effect from not only RAI but also from a predisposing condition may exist. The dose–response showed a statistically significant uptrend for cancer incidence with increasing administered RAI activity when the groups of <309 MBq, 309 to 504 MBq, and ≥505 MBq were analyzed (regression coefficient 1.13, 95% CI 1.06-1.21). On the other hand, high radiation doses to the thyroid exceeding 30 to 40 Gy decrease the risk of developing thyroid cancer although do not fully eliminate it. Therefore, RAI therapy may produce oppositely directed effects: one elevates the chance of thyroid cancer, and the other diminishes it. Nevertheless, the overall risk for developing thyroid cancer after RAI therapy remains, and patients treated with RAI for hyperthyroidism need to be followed up on a regular basis. Difference Between External and Internal Radiation Historically, in 1950s to 1970s, there was a long-standing belief that external exposure to X-rays is more effective in inducing thyroid carcinogenesis than internal irradiation with a “comparable” dose from 131 I. This was mostly based on the effects of RAI therapy where doses to the thyroid were on the order of tens to hundreds Grays and rarely resulted in thyroid malignancies while those from ≤1 Gy of external X-rays for medical indications led to elevated risk of thyroid cancer ( ). Apparently similar observations were seen in laboratory animals ( ). These differences were initially ascribed to different dose rates and distribution from the 2 types of exposure. Perhaps the best comparison of carcinogenic effects of the external and internal exposure can be drawn from radiation risks calculated in the studies of external childhood irradiation and in the population exposed to the Chornobyl fallouts. Risk Factors and Risk Modifiers in Radiation-Related Thyroid Cancer While the dose-dependent risk for thyroid cancer was well-proven and measured in different studies of irradiated groups (although using different risk metrics depending on the settings and in different dose intervals), some works also addressed the question whether there are other risk factors and/or modifiers of risk magnitude. These may be, for instance, demographic characteristics such as sex, age at exposure and at thyroid cancer diagnosis (if occurs), time since exposure, lifestyle and dietary habits, and various environmental exposures. In the Taiwanese study of thyroid cancer risk from CT scans, the effect of exposure was apparently independent of age and sex, and it was elevated in both males and females, and in all age groups of adults included in the study ( ). A study in Korea demonstrated that the effect of CT scan number was independent of body mass index, smoking status, history of other malignancies, and baseline Charlson Comorbidity Index ( ). In studies of external irradiation for childhood malignancies, older age at diagnosis of primary cancer and female sex were risk factors for thyroid cancer ( ). Statistically significant modifying effects of age at exposure, attained age (risk declines at older age), and time since exposure were found, but no effects for sex were detected ( , , ). The risk for thyroid cancer after external exposure was highest 25 to 29 years after irradiation, and remained elevated even 50 years later ( ). In a study of low-dose exposures, the highest RR was observed for the period <20 years since exposure and persisted 45+ years later ( ). A higher risk for thyroid cancer was found in females and for exposures at a younger age in the first screening of the Chornobyl UkrAm cohort in 1998-2000 ( ). However, there was no evidence of interaction of these parameters with the dose. In the follow-up analysis that used the data collected up to May, 2007, when some cohort members were screened up to 4 times, no modifying effects of sex, age, time since exposure, iodine prophylaxis, and tumor size were detected ( ) in line with the earlier work. Nonetheless, the estimates of dose-dependent risk declined from 5.25 (EOR 95% CI 1.70-27.5) in the first screening to 1.91 (ERR 95% CI 0.43-6.34) about a decade later, which may be suggestive of some age-related trends. In the Belarusian–American (BelAm) cohort, sex, age at exposure, urinary iodine concentration, and tumor size did not modify radiation risk ( ). In the case–control study with participants from Belarus and Russia, the radiation dose–adjusted parameters such as family history of thyroid cancer, increased body mass index, stable iodine deficiency status, and stable iodine supplementation conferred statistically significant risk for thyroid cancer, but except for iodine supplementation (which decreased the radiation effect), none of these factors, as well as sex and age at accident, were risk modifiers ( P heterogeneity > .15 for all) ( ). The only cohort study from Russia reported sex and time since exposure as modifiers of the radiation effect, and elevated risk was found only in subjects exposed at age <17 years but not in older individuals ( ). In view of evidence from different studies indicating that radiation dose, sex, age at exposure, and time since exposure affect the risk of developing thyroid cancer per se and may interact, it would be important to combine all the effects and obtain an integrative estimate of the role of radiation in an individual cancer case. This has been performed ( ), and free software is currently available at the US NCI/NIH website ( https://radiationcalculators.cancer.gov/irep/ ). The Interactive RadioEpidemiological Program – Probability of Cancer Causation from Radiation provides percentile estimates of the impact of exposure, which can be interpreted as “what was the contribution of radiation to the development of a tumor” in a given patient. Risks From Low-Dose Exposures Low doses are commonly defined as those below 0.1 Gy, and moderate are in the 0.1 to 1 Gy range ( , ). Low radiation doses to the thyroid may be received due to various exposure situations including planned or existing ones, or even in an emergency, and may be of occupational, medical, and public categories. Since the excess risk is proportional to the dose, low doses would expectedly bring about a small number of additional thyroid cancer cases above the background. Therefore, studies with a limited number of enrolled subjects and with relatively short follow-up times may have insufficient power to assess dose–response or result in unstable (ie, with wide errors corridors) estimates, which may be misleading. That is why the most reliable results are expected from pooled analyses. Furthermore, a careful consideration of works to be incorporated into a pooled study or a meta-analysis is essential ( , , , ). To date, a few studies have reported the dose–response for thyroid cancer in the low-dose range. The possibility of risk for cancer even from a low-dose thyroid irradiation, particularly in children, should be borne in mind, and all possible measures need to be taken to minimize exposures. The #4 reactor was completely destroyed by steam explosions, which caused the largest release of radioactive substances into the environment, and substantial amounts of them were deposited on mainly current territories of 3 states, Belarus, Ukraine, and Russia. The overall survival rate was excellent (more than 99%). In 2006, the World Health Organization estimated that there have been about 15 deaths due to radiation exposure in a combined cohort of 4837 cases: 10- to 15-year cause-specific mortality of about 0.3% ( ). However, recurrence rate was high (about 30-40%), even though follow-up periods in reported series were relatively short. Treatment results were reported in several works. Rumyantsev et al assessed factors associated with disease recurrence in 172 cases of radiation-associated PTCs and 325 sex- and age-matched sporadic PTCs from Russia ( ). They demonstrated that none of the tested variables interacted with radiation, suggesting that common treatment approaches for PTC patients are recommended regardless of a history of radiation exposure, in line with a report on thyroid cancer in externally irradiated patients ( ). The probability of locoregional and distant relapses was significantly lower in patients with total thyroidectomy and RAI treatment. For distant relapse after total thyroidectomy, the refusal to receive RAI treatment and age <15 years old at presentation were independent risk factors on a multivariate analysis. These findings suggest that it is important to provide standard therapy for radiation-associated thyroid cancer patients. Pathology The histological type of radiation-induced thyroid cancer is almost exclusively PTC. PTCs developed within the first decade after the accident demonstrated a higher proportion of solid pattern, and the tumors in the second decade and later were mainly classic papillary and follicular variant types ( ). An important question is whether there are any histopathological differences between radiation-induced and sporadic thyroid cancer. Bogdanova et al compared 2 age-matched groups: patients who were aged 4 years or less at the time of the accident and lived in the 3 most contaminated regions of Ukraine (radiation-associated), and those who were born after 1987, assuring that they were not exposed to 131 I from the accident (sporadic) ( ). This study included 301 radiation-associated and 194 sporadic PTCs subdivided into 3 age groups: children (≤ 14 years old), adolescents (15-18 years old), and adults (19-28 years old) at surgery. Among children, the radiation-associated PTCs had a significantly higher frequency of a dominant solid trabecular structure (in turn, a lower frequency of dominant papillary structure), intrathyroidal spread, extrathyroidal extension, and lymphatic/vascular invasion, indicative of higher aggressiveness, compared with sporadic PTCs. In all the age groups, the dominant papillary pattern and oxyphilic changes were less frequent in the radiation-associated PTCs. A significant age-related trend for dominant growth pattern (increasing of papillary structure and decreasing of solid structure) was seen in the radiation-associated PTCs but not in sporadic PTCs. These findings also suggest that even after exposure at a very young age, histological characteristics of adult-onset (radiation-associated) PTC approach those of sporadic PTCs. Molecular Studies Generally, the major driver oncogenes found in PTC are RET/PTC fusions, RAS mutations, and the BRAF mutation ( ). These genetic alterations occur in a mutually exclusive fashion, suggesting that constitutive activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling pathway, which is a common downstream cascade, plays a major role in the carcinogenesis of PTC ( ). The RET/PTC fusions are formed by chromosomal rearrangement of the C-terminal kinase domain of RET and the N-terminus of a partner gene. So far, at least 19 different types of RET/PTC fusions have been identified according to different partner genes. RET/PTC1 ( CCDC6-RET ) and RET/PTC3 ( NCO4-RET ) are the most common types, both of which are intrachromosomal inversions in chromosome 10 accounting for more than 90% of all RET/PTC fusions. The N-terminal domain usually promotes dimerization, leading to autophosphorylation of key tyrosine residues in the kinase domain of RET, and resulting in constitutive activation of RET. The frequency of RET/PTC in adult sporadic PTCs is 5% to 10%, and RET/PTC1 is predominant ( , ). On the other hand, its frequency in pediatric sporadic PTCs is high (25-65%) ( ). Soon after the discovery of increased incidence of childhood PTCs around Chornobyl, very high frequencies of RET/PTC were reported in those tumors ( ). Subsequent studies revealed that the frequencies of RET/PTC in tumors developed within 10 years and after 10 years were 64% to 86% and approximately 50%, respectively ( ). In addition, RET/PTC3 was more frequent in tumors developed 4 to 8 years after the accident (short latency), whereas RET/PTC1 was predominant in tumors with longer latency ( ). There was a close link between the type of RET/PTC ( RET/PTC3 or RET/PTC1 ) and histomorphology ( , ). RET/PTC3 was strongly associated with solid pattern, and RET/PTC1 was detected mainly in tumors with classic papillary structure. This was recapitulated in transgenic mouse models ( , ). While the latencies of the thyroid cancer cases following the Chornobyl accident were very short and the tumors were almost certainly radiation-induced, the reasons for such short latencies are not entirely clear; it took only 4 or 5 years from the presumably first hit in a single cell. Nakamura proposed an interesting hypothesis regarding radiation-associated leukemia ( ). Spontaneous occurring of fusion genes specific to acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) was found more frequently than the number of actual ALL cases. In addition, the clonal expansion of the cell having the fusion was often detected in individuals who do not develop ALL. Therefore, it was hypothesized that radiation-induced ALL may be developed from a small number of individuals who already had such a clone which expanded to a certain size. There is no such evidence for radiation-induced PTCs; however, it was reported that RET/PTC was detected in benign adenomas and Hashimoto thyroiditis tissues ( , ), although these findings remain controversial. Assuming that there already were thyroid follicular cells with RET/PTC (or other fusions), radiation might have played a role of a promoter rather than initiator, making short latency possible. Evolution of the Chornobyl Thyroid Cancer Over Time The Chornobyl accident occurred in 1986, and 37 years have passed since then. The incidence of thyroid cancer among exposed individuals has remained high. Therefore, relatively recent cases are not childhood or adolescent PTCs but adult PTCs with a history of radiation exposure during childhood or adolescence. Over the years, the proportion of true radiation-induced PTCs decreases, and that of tumors with the BRAF mutation increases. Zurnadzhy et al analyzed clinicopathological features of 247 radiation-associated and 138 sporadic PTCs from young (≤28 years old at diagnosis) Ukrainian patients ( ). In both groups, PTCs with BRAF V600E had a dominant papillary growth pattern, smaller size, and lower frequencies of major indicators of tumor aggressiveness (except for the Ki-67 labeling index) compared with the BRAF V600E -negative PTCs. Among the BRAF V600E -positive PTCs there was virtually no difference between the 2 groups. They concluded that BRAF V600E was not associated with more aggressive features in young patients regardless of etiology. The clinicopathological differences between radiation-associated and sporadic PTCs from young patients were observed in the BRAF V600E -negative PTCs. The same group extended their analysis of radiation-associated PTCs ( ). They included 428 PTC cases aged 4-49 years at surgery who lived in the 6 most contaminated regions of Ukraine, were ≤18 years old at the time of the accident, and underwent surgery in 1990-2017, covering the 30-year period after the accident. As the frequency of the BRAF V600E mutation has increased over the years, they focused on differences depending on its mutational status. In this study, the probability of causation of tumor development due to radiation exposure was also calculated. The BRAF V600E positivity was associated with older age at exposure and at surgery, longer latency, and lower probability of causation. The BRAF V600E -positive tumors had significantly smaller tumor size, higher Ki-67 labeling index, and more frequent oncocytic changes, multifocality, and dominant papillary growth pattern. Tumor invasiveness was less pronounced in the BRAF V600E -positive tumors and did not change with the probability of causation levels. However, BRAF V600E was a risk factor for recurrence, namely RAI-refractory metastasis. These findings suggest that no particular recommendations are necessary for the management of the BRAF V600E -positive PTC patients who are at middle age and have a history of radiation exposure. recapitulates major histopathological, molecular, and dose-related changes of the Chornobyl PTC in time to illustrate its evolution. Genetic Susceptibility Genetic background, namely single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) have been demonstrated to contribute to the risk for development of various diseases. In 2009, the first genome-wide association study reporting the genetic loci associated with predisposition to adult sporadic thyroid cancer in the European populations was performed ( ). The 2 strongest association signals were detected (rs965513 on chr 9q22.33 and rs944289 on chr 14q13.3). Interestingly, 9q22 and 14q13 include 2 thyroid-related genes, FOXE1 ( TTF2 ) and NKX2-1 ( TTF1 ), respectively. Later, long noncoding RNAs, PTCSC2 and PTCSC3 located in 9q22 and 14q13, respectively, were found, both of which were suggested to work as tumor suppressors ( ). The only case–control genome-wide association study using the Chornobyl cases and controls was published in 2010 ( ). Takahashi et al used 667 PTCs and 1275 controls and found that rs965513 on 9q22.33 was the strongest risk marker ( P -value: 4.8 × 10 −12 , OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.43-1.91), which was the same one found in sporadic PTCs (described above). On the other hand, no association between radiation-associated PTCs and rs944289 on 14q13.3 was detected. The large-scale and comprehensive genetic study for the Chornobyl PTCs described in the previous subsection ( ) also analyzed the associations of SNPs which were found in sporadic PTCs. The polygenic risk score using 12 SNPs was calculated and analyzed with radiation dose. Interestingly, PTC cases with 0 or lower radiation doses were more likely to have higher polygenic risk score ( P = 4.7 × 10 −4 ). This implies that PTC cases with higher doses may have other predisposing factors. In this study, albeit underpowered, 3 possible associations with radiation dose were also detected: rs1588635 (9q22.33; P = .012), rs2289261 (15q22.33, SMAD3 ; P = .030), and rs10069690 (5p15.33, TERT ; P = .054). In addition, there was no association with rare potentially protein-damaging variants in genes and pathways related to thyroid or other cancer predisposition, clinical radiation sensitivity syndromes, and DNA damage response. This controversy with the above studies needs to be addressed in the future research. At present, no germline genetic variants specifically associated with radiation-related thyroid cancer are known. Approximately 1.2 × 10 17 Bq (120 PBq) of 131 I was estimated to be released, and this amount was about 10% of that from the Chornobyl accident ( , ). The number of direct measurements of thyroid doses from short-lived RAI was very limited in the aftermath of the accident because of massive and widespread destructions. So far, various estimates of thyroid exposure doses have been made, and according to the latest study ( ), the median and 95th percentile of thyroid equivalent doses of 1-year-old children from 7 municipalities in the evacuation area ranged from 0.6 to 16 mSv and from 7.5 to 30 mSv, respectively. The variability in dose estimates was due not only to different contamination levels at different locations but also to different evacuation scenarios and behavioral patterns. These values seem to be lower than previous estimates by UNSCEAR ( ), in which the average thyroid doses at 1 year ranged 33-83 mSv. Improved methodology and considering typical Japanese iodine-rich diet are the main reasons for this ( ). Steinhauser et al indicated that the governmental efforts in the food monitoring campaign were successful in cutting the thyroid doses ( ). These doses are apparently far lower than those estimated after the Chornobyl accident, and the increase in the incidence of thyroid cancer due to radiation exposure is unlikely ( ). However, it may be possible that a very limited number of children received 50 to 100 mSv to the thyroid, which is not too a low dose. In the second round, the numbers of subjects and participants were 381 237 and 270 552, respectively, and 71 were classified as malignant or suspicious for malignancy (male: 32, female: 39). In the third round, the numbers of subjects and participants were 336 667 and 217 922, respectively, and 31 were classified as malignant or suspicious for malignancy (male: 13, female: 18). Of the 31, 29 were surgically diagnosed as thyroid carcinoma (all PTCs). In the fourth round, the numbers of subjects and participants were 294 237 and 183 352, respectively, and 36 were malignant or suspicious for malignancy (male: 16, female: 20). The number of surgically treated patients was 29, all diagnoses were PTC ( ). As of March 2022, confirmatory examinations are still in progress. These rates are apparently higher than previous rates of childhood and adolescent thyroid cancer in Japan. This is thought to be due to large-scale screening using high-resolution ultrasound equipment as discussed below. So far, an obvious increase in the incidence of thyroid cancer after 4 to 5 years of the accident has not been observed. Interestingly, obesity was positively associated with the thyroid cancer incidence ( ). Clinical, Pathological, and Molecular Findings Most of the surgical operations were performed in Fukushima Medical University. Clinicopathological findings of 125 cases, which were found in the first and second rounds of the FTE, were reported ( ). The sex ratio was 1:1.8 (male:female). The age range at surgery was 9-23 (mean 17.8) years, and the age range at the accident was 5-18 (mean 14.8) years. Total thyroidectomy and hemithyroidectomy were performed in 8.8% and 91.2%, respectively. By the pathological TNM classification (AJCC 7th edition), pT1a, pT1b, pT2, pT3, and pT4 were 34.4%, 24.8%, 1.6%, 39.2%, and 0%, respectively. Regarding lymph node status, pN0, pN1a, and pN1b were 22.4%, 60.8%, and 16.8%, respectively. Note that lateral lymph node dissection was performed only in cases with clinically evident positive lymph nodes. Distant metastasis was found in 3 cases (2.4%). Of the 125 cases, 121 were pathologically diagnosed as PTC, 3 were poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma, and 1 was under debate. Among the 121 PTCs, 110 was classic type, 4 were follicular variant, 3 were diffuse sclerosing variant, and 4 were cribriform-morular variant, which is the typical pattern observed in familial adenomatous polyposis. Iwadate et al also reported similar clinicopathological findings of 138 cases, most of which overlapped with the previous study ( ). In 2015, the first genetic study was reported ( ). Tronko et al observed that many thyroid cancer cases had occurred in people who were 0-5 years old at the time of the Chornobyl accident, but no cases had occurred in people who were 0-5 years old at the time of the Fukushima accident ( ). In terms of the pathological findings, radiation-associated PTCs in Ukraine demonstrated the higher frequency of tumors with a dominant solid-trabecular pattern, higher invasiveness, more frequent extrathyroidal extension, and lymphatic/vascular invasion compared with sporadic PTCs in the same area ( ). However, these differences were not found between the Fukushima PTCs and age-matched PTCs from other prefectures in Japan ( ). In addition, when the Fukushima cases were divided into 2 groups, those treated during the first 4 years and later (like Chornobyl), there were no histopathological differences between the 2 groups ( ). As mentioned above, the driver oncogenes predominantly found in tumors after the Chornobyl accident were RET/PTC s, especially in cases with short latency. By contrast, the BRAF V600E mutation is the most prevalent oncogene in the Fukushima cases. All of these differences suggest that the Fukushima PTCs are not radiation-related cancers. However, it is important to note that most of the Chornobyl cases were diagnosed more than 5 years after the accident, while many of the reported Fukushima cases were found less than 5 years after the accident. Therefore, careful observation and analyses are still needed in the future. Disputable Issues Regarding the radiation dose and the incidence of thyroid cancer, there are several conflicting reports regarding an association between air dose and the incidence ( , ); however, internal exposure doses were not correlated with air doses ( ), and the issue of ecological fallacy in these studies has been pointed out. Ohira et al used average thyroid doses which were calculated by the combination of external and internal exposures and reported the lack of association between the thyroid doses and cancer incidence ( ). So far, there is no evidence that radiation from the accident has caused thyroid cancers in Fukushima. However, well-designed epidemiological studies, for instance those considering individual thyroid doses/case–control studies, are needed. Although the FTE was started as a measure against residents’ anxiety about radiation health effects but not to reduce the number of cancer deaths as regular cancer screening, after accumulating data described above, the FTE has raised another issue: to continue or discontinue the FTE. This is because many PTCs are slow growing in nature, and there are many indolent/occult cancers. There are different arguments. Lymph node metastasis was found in 78% of the cases ( ), indicating that many of these tumors were invasive. Midorikawa et al compared tumor diameters between the screening and confirmatory examinations in the first round of the FTE and found that 76% of the tumors did not grow although most of the time intervals between 2 measurements were up to 1 year ( ). They also suggested a growth arrest pattern after growing for years. On the other hand, Takahashi et al built a cancer-progression model based on the National Cancer Registry data in Japan and demonstrated that the number of observed thyroid cancer cases found in the FTE was within the 95% CIs of the expected number of cases, with median sojourn times (the duration of the preclinical yet screen-detectable phase of a tumor) of 34 (for males) and 30 (for females) years ( ). This experience would be useful not only in case of a nuclear accident but for management of PTCs in young age. Reducing Thyroid Cancer Risk From Radiation Exposure External At present, almost all external irradiation of the thyroid occurs as planned medical exposures of patients or occupational exposures of medical personnel, nuclear workers, or researchers. Diagnostic exposures usually deliver relatively low doses to the thyroid; however, repeated examinations, especially in children, require caution. In 1977, the ICRP introduced the principle “As Low As Reasonably Achievable” (ALARA) to balance the risks and benefits ( ), and this has become the standard approach. In ALARA, economic and social factors are also taken into account. The American Thyroid Association issued “Policy Statement on Thyroid Shielding During Diagnostic Medical and Dental Radiology” in 2013 ( ). According to this policy, clinicians are recommended to adequately acquire the information regarding the potential risks of radiation and radiation dosimetry, especially for children and to the thyroid. Before performing a diagnostic exposure, consideration of the necessity, potential risks and benefits, and alternative methods are recommended. For mammography, thyroid shields are not recommended because of extremely low doses to the thyroid. Regarding CT scans, other radiographies and dental X-rays, the use of thyroid shields is recommended when possible to reduce thyroid dose without compromising the goal of the examination. Thyroid shielding during CT examinations of the neck area, chest, and cervical spine was proposed 2 decades ago, and found to reduce thyroid exposure by about 70% ( ). A 40% to 60% dose reduction was achieved with the thyroid shield at brain CT ( ). Schneider et al summarized the recent publications on thyroid collars in dental radiology. Reduction rates of thyroid doses by thyroid shielding in intraoral radiographs, panoramic radiographs, cephalometric radiographs, and cone beam CT were 27% to 59%, 9.8% to 23.7%, 85%, and 45.9%, respectively ( ). Protection of the thyroid for medical staff involved in different types of interventional radiological procedures which may deliver scattered radiation is commonly achieved by wearing a neck collar or an apron with thyroid coverage. These protective garments, usually corresponding to the 0.35- to 0.5-mm-thick layer of lead, reduce the equivalent dose to the thyroid by a factor from 5 to 10 ( ). Other means of protection of interventionalists may be freestanding adjustable over-table shields or ceiling-mounted shields, and disposable lead-free drapes. Exposures of medical staff should also be minimized in line with the ALARA principle. The dose to the thyroid (as well as to other tissues) can be reduced by shortening the time of a procedure, which assumes the operator experience, training and preparedness to a given procedure/patient, usage of appropriate imaging equipment and minimizing the number of images, and, during the procedure, positioning in a less exposed to scattered radiation area and usage of protective shielding. Similar considerations are applicable to researchers dealing with open sources of penetrating ionizing radiation. Family members or caretakers of patients after RAI therapy can minimize their exposures by maintaining appropriate physical distance and minimizing time of direct contact. Internal Iodine is an essential component of thyroid hormones, and the majority of iodine in the human body is accumulated in the thyroid gland. While in the past certain populations might have experienced exposures to RAI through inhalation or ingestion because of living in the areas affected by the detonations at nuclear test sites or releases from nuclear facilities (see section “Public Exposures” above), current everyday scenarios of internal exposure to RAI are rather limited to those for patients in clinical settings or researchers using RAI. everyday scenarios of internal exposure to RAI are rather limited to those for patients in clinical settings or researchers using RAI. For patients receiving RAI-containing radiopharmaceuticals, when the thyroid is not a target organ, iodine thyroid blocking (ITB), an oral administration of stable iodine, may be considered and recommended in the case of high activities to be administered, and especially if iodine release or leakage from the radiopharmaceuticals is a concern. Researchers dealing with RAI may inhale some isotope during experiments or contaminate the skin. Simple measures such as wearing protective gloves, glasses, and masks or respirators, working in the fume hood and thorough monitoring of contamination would be effective in preventing the thyroid from internal exposure. Since RAI is the byproduct of fission of uranium atoms, it is formed in nuclear reactors employing the uranium fuel, which is the most common type of fuel used in nuclear power plants ( ). Under normal operating conditions, negligible or no RAI is released from nuclear power plants. However, a nuclear accident at the acting reactor is the most serious situation that may cause massive release of RAI into the environment following which large populations may be exposed. The major pathways of RAI internalization to organisms are inhalation and ingestion of radiocontaminated food and water. Sheltering and/or evaluation from the radionuclide-contaminated areas and wearing masks may help to reduce RAI uptake through inhalation. An appropriate countermeasure to radiation exposure in case of nuclear reactor accident is ITB. In part, because stable iodine and RAI are chemically and biochemically identical, the former stoichiometrically competes with RAI and prevents its incorporation to the thyroid, thus reducing the risk for thyroid cancer among people exposed to RAI released from the accident. In 2017, the World Health Organization updated guidelines for ITB in case of nuclear emergencies ( ). The followings are important points: the optimal timing of ITB is less than 24 hours prior to and up to 2 hours after the expected onset of exposure, and ITB up to 8 hours may still be reasonable. However, starting ITB later than 24 hours may be more harmful than beneficial because of extending biological half-life of RAI already accumulated to the thyroid. A single administration is usually sufficient. However, in case of prolonged (more than 24 hours) or repeated exposure (eg, unavoidable ingestion of contaminated food/drink, evacuation is not possible), repeated ITB may be needed. It should be noted that neonates, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and older adults (>60 years old) should not receive ITB repeatedly. Children, adolescents, and pregnant and breastfeeding women are most likely to benefit from ITB, whereas there would be little benefit to adults over the age of 40. People living in iodine-deficient regions may be more susceptible to RAI. Decision on ITB should be issued by the local authorities based on the analysis of radiological situation. ITB should not be considered as a stand-alone method to prevent exposure to RAI. Other actions such as evacuation and sheltering, and restriction of contaminated food/drink consumption should be implemented. Indeed, after the accident at Fukushima Dai-ichi Nuclear Power Plant, food monitoring was successful in reducing thyroid doses in contrast to Chornobyl. Another dramatic scenario of possible mass exposure to RAI is by a nuclear weapon. For example, RAI isotopes from the 16-kiloton uranium A-bomb in Hiroshima lasted from about a day ( 134 I), a week ( 133 I, 135 I) to about a month ( 131 I, 132 I) ( ). Given that RAI is formed after a nuclear blast, ITB might seem reasonable, but no official documents substantiating this measure are available. It should also be understood that ITB, if performed timely, protects the thyroid only from the internal exposure to RAI, but not from external penetrating radiation by γ-rays and neutrons, which is the major primary radiation-related damaging factor of a uranium- or plutonium-based nuclear device and a principal one of a thermonuclear device. The number of immediate deaths and those occurring within a year after the attack far outweighs that of thyroid cancers that may potentially develop later. Stable iodine does not protect the thyroid from other types of radionuclides inhaled or ingested, when they affect the organism internally. The only proper way of protecting the thyroid from mass-destruction nuclear weapon is sheltering, avoiding skin/eye/airway/digestive tract exposures, and evacuation/escape from the affected area as soon as possible. Similar considerations apply to the scenarios of a “dirty bomb” (a “radiological dispersal device”) or a destruction of spent fuel/radioactive waste storages which may cause heavy contamination of the territory but would not produce RAI isotopes in the absence of atomic fission. Perspectives of Studies in Radiation-Related Thyroid Cancer A substantial progress in understanding of radiation-related thyroid cancer has been achieved since the discovery of this phenomenon about 60 years ago. Irradiation of the head, neck, and chest areas has been learned to increase the risk for developing thyroid malignancy during the lifespan. This stimulated numerous investigations in medical, industrial, and military settings whenever radiation exposure was relevant. Radiation risks have been quantified and found to be comparable for the external and internal radiation. According to this knowledge, certain groups at elevated risk could be determined, including those with medical, occupational, or emergency exposures. Now, the focus of radiation risk studies is shifting toward low-dose exposures in view of growing number of various radiological procedures, especially in pediatric patients ( ). The markers of radiation-related thyroid cancer have not been found so far. Overlaps in the histological types, oncogenic driver spectrums, and corresponding gene expression profiles between radiation-related and sporadic tumors suggest that these parameters were unlikely to serve as a marker. A recent next generation sequencing-based study of the Chornobyl PTCs reported a dose-dependent increase in small deletions and simple/balanced structural variants, which might have formed after double-stand DNA breaks ( ). These clonal events may be a promising candidate for becoming a molecular marker of radiation relatedness of a tumor, and more investigations in independent series would be of great interest. Genetic predisposition to developing thyroid cancer after irradiation is insufficiently explored. As yet, no radiation-specific germline variants have been found. The relationships of individual variants with the dose have been poorly addressed so far and were limited to the selected SNPs associated with sporadic thyroid cancer in 1 study ( ). Whether the genetic variants may modify the dose effect is not established, but may be addressed using different risk models, including time to event ones, in which the individual doses would be incorporated. Furthermore, it is unknown if predisposing germline variants other than SNPs (eg, structural variations) may exist; this may require deeper genomic research employing new technologies (eg, long-read sequencing). It would also be important to clarify if exposures to additional environmental factors may be a risk factor or modify the risk ( ), and whether gene–environment interactions could play a role in radiation-related thyroid cancer. Clinical studies have demonstrated that thyroid cancers diagnosed in irradiated patients are of the same histological types as in nonirradiated patients and that disease prognosis is determined by tumor characteristics regardless of etiology. This is rather good news for clinicians to know that standard treatment and follow-up approaches could be used for radiation-exposed patients, but it is necessary to keep in mind that thyroid cancer phenotype is changing with patient age and latency period. While it is known that thyroid cancers have more aggressive clinicopathological features in children with a radiation history than in nonexposed and that the difference becomes less pronounced in patients of middle age, it needs to be established whether this trend remains stable and whether thyroid cancer in older patients exposed to radiation in childhood would not develop more aggressive or RAI-refractory tumors after a longer latency. The cohorts of the atomic bomb survivors in Japan, the population exposed due to the Chornobyl accident, and patients who had received radiological procedures in childhood need to be closely followed-up and studied using the best medical, ethical, and epidemiological practices.
